title: Head Lice in Kids: A Pediatrician's Guide
summary: Head lice in kids? Learn how to tell lice from dandruff, treat them safely by age, clean up without overdoing it, and know when to call your pediatrician.
body_markdown:
Head lice are tiny insects that live in hair and spread through head-to-head contact. They cause itching but are not dangerous and are not a sign of poor hygiene. Most cases are treated at home with an over-the-counter lice medicine and careful combing. This guide shows you how to spot lice, treat them safely, and know when to call your pediatrician.


Think it might be lice? A Blueberry pediatrician can walk you through the check tonight.


[Start a visit](https://app.blueberrypediatrics.com/bbjoin?show_monthly_kit_30=true)


## Key Takeaways


- Head lice are not dangerous, and they are not a sign of poor hygiene or a dirty home.
- Lice spread mainly by direct head-to-head contact. Pets do not carry or spread them, and hats and furniture are a much smaller risk than head-to-head contact.
- Treat lice with an age-appropriate over-the-counter lice medicine, plus careful combing.
- School-age children do not need to be sent home or kept home. A younger child in child care can finish the day, as long as treatment starts before they go back the next morning.
- "No-nit" policies are discouraged by the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), the CDC, and the National Association of School Nurses.


## What are head lice?


Head lice are tiny, wingless insects that live close to the scalp and feed on small amounts of blood. About the size of a sesame seed, they do not carry disease and are not a health hazard. Getting them does not mean your child or your home is dirty.


Lice are very common in young children. The CDC estimates there are 6 to 12 million infestations each year among children ages 3 to 11 in the United States. The main problem they cause is itching, plus a lot of parent stress. The stigma is often harder on families than the bugs themselves.


Adult lice lay their eggs, called nits, close to the scalp where it is warm.


## How do I know if my child has lice? (Symptoms)


The most common sign is an itchy scalp, especially behind the ears and at the back of the neck. But itching can take weeks to start, and some children never itch at all, so the surest way to know is to look closely.


Here is what to look for:


- Itching behind the ears or at the nape of the neck.
- Small tan or brown insects moving in the hair. Adult lice move fast and avoid light.
- Tiny eggs (nits) glued to the hair close to the scalp.
- A tickling feeling, like something is moving in the hair.
- Trouble sleeping, since lice are more active in the dark.


Check the hair in bright light, parting it in small sections and looking close to the scalp, starting behind the ears and at the nape of the neck. A fine-tooth comb makes lice and nits easier to find.


### Nits vs. dandruff: how to tell the difference


The easiest way to tell nits from dandruff is the flick test. Nits are glued to the hair and do not brush or flick off. Dandruff and dry-skin flakes slide off easily.


In our telehealth visits, parents often ask how to tell lice from ordinary dandruff. Here is the rule we share:


- Nits are tiny oval eggs, tan or yellow-white. Live nits sit within about 1 cm of the scalp, roughly a finger's width. You cannot slide them off with your fingers.
- Dandruff is white, sits loosely, and moves or falls off easily.


Nits within about 1 cm of the scalp point to an active or recent case. Nits farther out on the hair are usually old and already hatched.


## How do head lice spread? (And common myths)


Head lice spread mainly through direct head-to-head contact. When two heads touch, they can crawl from one child's hair to another's, which is why they spread during play, sports, sleepovers, and selfies. Lice have no wings, so they cannot jump or fly, and pets do not carry or spread them (CDC).


That clears up two other common myths:


- Myth: Lice mean a dirty house. They are not a sign of being dirty. Clean hair gets them just as easily.
- Myth: You easily catch lice from hats and furniture. This is uncommon. Lice do not survive long off the scalp, so shared objects are a much smaller risk than head-to-head contact.


Can one child give lice to the whole family? Yes, through close contact at home, so check everyone in the house on the same day.


## How do I get rid of head lice? Step-by-step treatment


Most cases are treated at home, and the plan is simple. Use an age-appropriate lice medicine exactly as directed, comb the hair to remove lice and nits, then repeat both over the next 2 to 3 weeks. There is no overnight fix, so plan for a patient, steady approach.


The right medicine depends on your child's age, so read the age rules carefully.


### Over-the-counter lice medicines (permethrin, pyrethrin, ivermectin lotion)


Over-the-counter (OTC) lice medicines are what most families try first. A pediculicide is a medicine that kills lice. Have an adult apply the product and follow the package directions exactly.


Lice medicine Youngest approved age Type Good to know


Permethrin 1% lotion 2 months OTC First-line choice. Retreat on day 9 to 10 if you still see live lice.


Pyrethrins with piperonyl butoxide 2 years OTC First-line choice. Retreat on day 9 to 10. Not for children under 2 years.


Ivermectin 0.5% lotion 6 months OTC Usually needs only one application.


Permethrin 1% lotion is approved for children 2 months and older. Pyrethrin products are approved only for children 2 years and older. Ivermectin 0.5% lotion is also over the counter, for children 6 months and older, and usually needs only one treatment. These three are not interchangeable, so always check the age on the product you choose.


Babies under 2 months


No lice medicine is FDA-approved for infants under 2 months old. Do not use any lice medicine on a baby this young. Call your pediatrician first. In the meantime (this is the one case where hand-removal and combing are the main tool), remove lice and nits gently by hand and with a fine-tooth comb.


Match the medicine to your child's age


Do not use a pyrethrin product on a child under 2 years, and do not use ivermectin lotion under 6 months. Using a lice medicine below its approved age can be unsafe. When in doubt, ask your pediatrician.


You may have heard that lice are becoming resistant to drugstore treatments. Some lice have developed resistance to permethrin. The CDC says how common this is remains unknown. Even so, the AAP still recommends permethrin and pyrethrin products as the first thing to try. There is no clear evidence that these genetic changes make the medicines fail in real life. If the first treatment does not work, that is worth a call to your pediatrician. It usually has a simpler cause than resistance.


### Wet-combing (the comb-out method)


Wet-combing means combing wet, conditioned hair with a fine-tooth nit comb to remove lice and nits and check whether treatment is working.


Be honest about what combing can do. The comb-out method usually does not work on its own to get rid of head lice (AAP). Combing helps remove nits, but it usually does not clear lice by itself. Use it alongside a lice medicine, not instead of one, unless your pediatrician suggests otherwise.


> The comb-out method usually doesn't work on its own to get rid of head lice.
>
>
> American Academy of Pediatrics


To wet-comb:


1. Wet the hair and add plenty of conditioner.
2. Comb small sections from the scalp to the ends.
3. Wipe the comb on a paper towel after each pass.
4. Check each section carefully.
5. Repeat every 2 to 3 days for 2 to 3 weeks.


### When to consider prescription treatment


Most families never need a prescription. But if OTC medicines truly do not work, your pediatrician may prescribe a stronger option. Prescription lice medicines include spinosad 0.9% (for children 6 months and older) and malathion 0.5% (for children 6 years and older).


Malathion age floor


Malathion 0.5% is only for children 6 years and older. It is the one lice medicine here with a school-age lower limit. Do not use it on a younger child.


There is also an oral prescription option, ivermectin taken by mouth, reserved for lice that resist all approved topical treatments.


If a first treatment does not seem to work, resistance is usually not the reason. The most common causes, in order, are:


1. A wrong diagnosis (it was not lice).
2. Not following the directions closely.
3. Not using enough medicine, or not retreating on time.
4. Reinfestation from someone else.


A quick call to your pediatrician can help you sort out which one it is.


## How do I clean my home after lice?


You do not need to deep-clean your whole house. Lice do not live long off the scalp, so heavy cleaning does not help. A few simple steps are enough:


- Wash recently used bedding, clothing, hats, and towels in hot water (130°F or hotter). Dry on high heat.
- Seal items you cannot wash in a plastic bag for 2 weeks.
- Soak combs and brushes in hot water (130°F or hotter) for 5 to 10 minutes.
- Vacuum where your child sat or lay down.


Skip household lice sprays and fumigants. They are not needed and expose your family to unnecessary chemicals. Focus on treating heads and combing hair, not scrubbing the house.


## When can my child go back to school? (The "no-nit" policy reality)


School-age children with lice do not need to be sent home early or kept home. This is the position of the AAP, the CDC, and the National Association of School Nurses. Your child can stay in class and return to school as usual.


By the time lice are found, a child has usually had them for 4 to 6 weeks, so they pose little new risk to classmates. The AAP notes head lice have low contagion in classrooms. Remind your child to avoid close head-to-head contact, but they do not need to miss school.


Child care is a little different. A younger child in child care can finish the day. No exclusion is needed, as long as treatment starts before they return the next morning.


"No-nit" policies keep children out of school until every nit is gone. They are discouraged by the AAP, the CDC, and the National Association of School Nurses. These policies cause missed school for no medical reason.


## When should I call the pediatrician? (And how telehealth helps)


Call your pediatrician if:


- You are not sure it is lice.
- Treatment does not seem to work.
- The scalp looks infected (red, tender, or oozing).
- Your child is under 2 months old.
- The itching or rash is still there more than a week after treatment.


Lice are also a great fit for a[telehealth visit](https://www.blueberrypediatrics.com/how-it-works) , especially during a busy school week.


Here is how[a Blueberry pediatrician can help by phone or chat](https://app.blueberrypediatrics.com/bbjoin?show_monthly_kit_30=true) . We can walk you through where and how to check your child's hair. We can review what you find and help you tell nits from dandruff and hair casts. We can pick a lice medicine that fits your child's age. And we can decide whether a prescription-only medicine is warranted.


One more reassurance: some itching is normal even after treatment works. Scalp itching or mild burning can last for many days after the lice are dead. That is not a reason to treat again right away.

## How can I prevent head lice?


You cannot prevent every case, and that is okay. The AAP notes it is unlikely all cases can be prevented, because children make head-to-head contact so often, and reinfestation is common. Still, a few habits lower the risk:


- Teach children to avoid direct head-to-head contact during play and sports.
- Avoid sharing brushes, combs, hats, and pillows.
- Do regular head checks, especially after sleepovers, camps, and the start of school.


One important balance: children should not refuse protective headgear, such as a bike or sports helmet, out of fear of head lice (AAP). A helmet prevents serious injury. A small chance of lice is not a reason to skip it.


## Your Head Lice Action Checklist


1. Confirm it's lice. Check behind the ears and at the nape of the neck for nits within about 1 cm of the scalp. Nits are glued to the hair and do not brush off the way dandruff does.
2. Choose an age-appropriate OTC lice medicine and have an adult apply it exactly as directed. Permethrin 1% is approved from 2 months, pyrethrins only from 2 years, and ivermectin 0.5% lotion from 6 months (usually one application).
3. Comb wet hair with a fine-tooth nit comb. Remove lice and nits section by section.
4. Recheck 8 to 12 hours after treatment. A few lice moving slowly is expected. Do not reapply the medicine; comb them out instead. Only if the lice look as active as before, and you find no dead ones, call your pediatrician before trying a second product.
5. Repeat treatment on the schedule the product or your pediatrician specifies (usually around day 9).
6. Keep combing every 2 to 3 days for 2 to 3 weeks until no lice are found.
7. Wash recently used bedding, clothing, and hats in hot water (130°F or hotter) and dry on high heat. Bag non-washable items for 2 weeks.
8. Check everyone in the house on the same day, and keep checking every 2 to 3 days. Treat anyone with live lice. Treat anyone with nits within about 1 cm of the scalp, roughly a finger's width. Also treat anyone who shares a bed with your child, even if you find no live lice on them.
9. Send your child back to school. School-age children do not need to be sent home or kept home. In child care, treatment can wait until the end of the day, with no exclusion needed, as long as it starts before the child goes back the next morning.
10. Prevent reinfestation. Avoid head-to-head contact and do not share brushes, hats, or pillows. At the same time, children should not refuse protective headgear, such as a helmet, out of fear of head lice.


## What about home remedies?


You may have heard that mayonnaise, olive oil, or tea tree oil can smother lice. These are not proven to kill lice and are not recommended. They can also be messy. What pediatricians recommend instead is an age-appropriate lice medicine plus careful combing.


Two "remedies" are never safe and should never go on your child's head.


Never use these on hair


Gasoline, kerosene, and products made for animals are never appropriate for head lice in humans. They can cause serious harm.


Skip vinegar and "nit-loosening" sprays


Vinegar and WD-40-style nit-loosening products do not work. They carry a risk of skin irritation and swallowing harm. Do not use them.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### What is the difference between nits and dandruff?


Nits are lice eggs glued to the hair within about 1 cm of the scalp; they do not brush off. Dandruff is loose and slides off easily.


### Can you get lice from pillows or hats?


Rarely. Lice spread mainly by direct head-to-head contact and do not survive long off the scalp.


### Can my child give lice to the whole family?


Yes, through close contact at home. Check everyone on the same day. Treat anyone with live lice, anyone with nits within about 1 cm of the scalp, and anyone who shares a bed with your child even if you find no live lice on them.


### What if the over-the-counter treatment doesn't work?


Usually the reason is a wrong diagnosis, not following directions, or reinfestation, not resistance. Call your pediatrician for next steps.


### When do I need a prescription lice treatment?


Only when OTC medicines and combing have truly failed. Your pediatrician can prescribe a stronger option for your child's age.


### Do I need to clean my whole house?


No. Wash recently used bedding and clothes in hot water, dry on high heat, and bag what you cannot wash for 2 weeks.


### When can my child go back to school?


Right away. School-age children do not need to be sent home or kept home for lice or nits.


### Are "no-nit" policies still a thing?


Some schools use them, but they are discouraged by the AAP, the CDC, and the National Association of School Nurses.


### Are head lice dangerous or a sign of being dirty?


No. They are not dangerous, do not spread disease, and are not a sign of poor hygiene. Anyone can get them.
